title: A Mutation Entry Does Not Decide Ownership: Supreme Court Restores Family's Co-Ownership Over Indore Land
meta_description: Supreme Court holds an unproved relinquishment and a revenue mutation entry cannot extinguish a co-owner's title, restoring a family's land rights.
bench: Justices Sanjay Karol and Augustine George Masih
body: Two brothers, Ramprasad and Vasudev, inherited 12.41 acres of agricultural land near Indore on the death of their father, Bhagwansingh. For years the land stood in both their names in the revenue record. Then Ramprasad's name was struck off and Vasudev was shown as the sole khatedar, on the strength of a relinquishment said to have been executed in Vasudev's favour. Ramprasad's legal heirs went to civil court saying no such relinquishment was ever made, and that the mutation recorded a transfer that never happened.

The trial court believed them. It decreed the suit in 2016, holding that the relinquishment document was not proved and that Ramprasad's share survived. The first appellate court affirmed that decree in 2019. Both courts read the oral and documentary evidence the same way: Vasudev could point to a mutation entry, but he could not produce a relinquishment deed that would stand up to scrutiny, registered or otherwise.

The Madhya Pradesh High Court took a different view in second appeal and reversed the concurrent findings, reinstating Vasudev's exclusive title. That is where the matter went wrong, the Supreme Court held. A second appeal under Section 100 of the Code of Civil Procedure exists to correct a substantial question of law, not to let a High Court re-weigh evidence that two courts below have already assessed consistently. The bench of Justices Sanjay Karol and Augustine George Masih found that the High Court had done exactly that, substituting its own appreciation of the relinquishment story for findings of fact it had no business disturbing.

On the substantive point, the Court restated something Indian property lawyers have argued for decades but revenue officials routinely forget: an entry in the record of rights is fiscal and administrative, made to assist in the collection of land revenue. It is not a document of title and it settles nothing about ownership. A patwari or a revenue officer recording a change of name, however official it looks on paper, cannot by itself operate as a conveyance, a release, or a relinquishment of proprietary rights. Those rights pass only through instruments the law recognises, typically a registered document where the value of the interest crosses the statutory threshold under the Registration Act and the Transfer of Property Act.

The Court went further and addressed what Vasudev's side had leaned on heavily: the fact that the relinquishment, even if informal, had gone unchallenged for years while the mutation stood. Long inaction does not cure a defective transfer, the bench held. Acquiescence might support an estoppel in some fact patterns, but where the core document relied upon is itself unproved, there is nothing for acquiescence to attach to. Allowing a disputed mutation to harden into title merely through the passage of time would let revenue records do the work the law assigns to conveyancing, which the Court was not prepared to permit.

On the result, the appeal succeeded. The Supreme Court set aside the High Court's 2025 judgment and restored the first appellate court's 2019 decree, which in turn had upheld the trial court's 2016 decree in Ramprasad's favour. The parties were left to work out separate possession between the co-owners, since a decree declaring co-ownership does not by itself partition the land on the ground. The Court also restrained the respondents from creating third-party rights over the disputed portion pending that partition, so the practical fight over who farms which part of the 12.41 acres is not over, only the question of title.

For practitioners the message is not new in substance, only in emphasis. Clients who rely on a mutation entry as their primary proof of ownership are relying on the weakest link in the chain. Anyone defending a title suit where the other side's whole case rests on a revenue record change should be asking, from the first hearing, where the actual conveyance or relinquishment document is, and whether it meets the formal requirements the law sets for transferring an interest in immovable property. This judgment gives that line of attack the Supreme Court's direct endorsement, in a fact situation, family land with a disputed relinquishment, that recurs constantly in Indian civil courts.
why_it_matters: Family partition and succession disputes in India routinely turn on patta or khatauni entries that one side treats as proof of title. This ruling confirms such entries are administrative, not proprietary, and that a High Court cannot reopen concurrent findings of fact in second appeal merely because it reads the same evidence differently. Litigators defending co-ownership claims now have a direct 2026 Supreme Court authority to counter title claims built solely on revenue records.
card_summary: Supreme Court holds a revenue mutation entry cannot create or extinguish title, and restores a family's co-ownership after the High Court wrongly reopened concurrent findings in second appeal.
card_tip: Never let a client's title defence rest on a mutation entry alone; demand the underlying registered conveyance or relinquishment deed before conceding anything.
